mcqs.question: Why is asking for a level change usually a higher-leverage move than asking for more base salary within your assigned level?
options: Recruiters are only allowed to discuss level, never base, until after the offer is signed
Base salary is fixed by law while levels are set entirely at the recruiter's discretion
A level change moves you into a different band entirely, while a recruiter usually has only narrow discretion to flex base or equity within your current band
Levels are renegotiated automatically every year, so pushing on base is the only real one-time lever
mcqs.explanation: A recruiter typically has real authority to move your base or equity within your assigned band, but changing the level itself requires the leveling committee to revisit scope — which is why it has to be raised early, and why it moves you to a different, usually larger, band rather than a marginal adjustment within one.

mcqs.question: Of base salary, bonus target percentage, and equity grant size, which is typically the most flexible lever for a recruiter to move on a first offer?
options: Bonus target percentage, since it's recalculated every negotiation round
Base salary, since it has no policy constraints at all
Equity grant size, since it's a one-time grant decision rather than a recurring cost tied to company-wide policy
None of the three are ever negotiable before a signed offer
mcqs.explanation: Bonus target percentages are usually set uniformly at the company or org level and rarely flex per candidate, while equity is a one-time grant decision a recruiter can usually adjust more freely — spending negotiation effort on a fixed bonus target wastes a round that could move the equity number instead.

mcqs.question: Why should you cross-reference at least two comp data sources before forming a target number, rather than anchoring on one levels.fyi data point?
options: Crowdsourced comp sites are always fake and should never be used
A single data point can be stale, self-reported inaccurately, or from a different location's cost-of-living adjustment, and anchoring hard on it risks losing credibility if it's wrong
Recruiters can see which website you used and penalize you for it
Comp data changes hourly, so any single lookup is obsolete by the time you negotiate
mcqs.explanation: The risk isn't that the data is fake, it's that any one number can be outdated or location-mismatched — cross-referencing your own network and the recruiter's stated band catches a bad anchor before you build your ask around it.

mcqs.question: Two offers have the same year-one total comp, but one is at a mid level and one is at a senior level. Why can the mid-level offer still be the worse long-term trade?
options: Mid-level offers always include worse benefits packages
Every future raise compounds off the level's base ceiling, so the lower band caps growth even if year-one totals currently match
Senior-level employees are legally guaranteed a raise every year
Mid-level offers can be revoked more easily than senior-level ones
mcqs.explanation: The level sets the band ceiling that all future raises compound against; a matching year-one number hides the fact that the mid-level band caps out lower, and a promotion to close that gap isn't guaranteed on any fixed timeline.

mcqs.question: What's the main flaw in the plan "take the lower level now, get promoted fast once I'm in"?
options: Promotions are usually gated by 12-24 months at your current level and a limited promotion budget, and a lower starting level also shapes your manager's early expectations toward lower-scoped work
Companies never promote anyone who was leveled down at hire
Taking a lower level voids your ability to negotiate base salary in the future
It's actually a good plan with no real downside
mcqs.explanation: Promotion cycles are slower and more competitive than onboarding optimism assumes, and a lower starting level tends to produce lower-scoped assignments early on, which undercuts the very evidence you'd need to build a promotion case.

mcqs.question: What's a practical signal that you should negotiate for a level change rather than just a higher number within your current band?
options: Your target number is inside the band one level up from the one you were offered
The recruiter mentioned levels.fyi during the call
You've been at the company for over a year
The signing bonus offered is below the industry average
mcqs.explanation: If your realistic target sits inside the next level's band rather than at the stretched top of your current one, pushing for an exception within the wrong band is harder to get approved than addressing the level directly, which has its own larger ceiling.
